lead: An engine makes two powers at once: indicated power at the piston face and brake power at the shaft. Only brake power is measured directly, with a brake. Indicated power comes from the p-V loop or a Morse test; friction power from the motoring test, Willans line or subtraction.
prereq: You need: the power and efficiency definitions in the chapter on performance parameters, and swept volume and the four-stroke cycle (see Four-stroke and two-stroke engines).

blocks.text: Power leaves an engine down the shaft. The gas first spends part of its work on the engine's own friction — bearings, rings, valve train, oil and water pumps — and only the remainder reaches the shaft. Three numbers therefore exist.

Indicated power IP is the rate of work done by the gas on the piston. Brake power BP is the rate of work at the shaft. Friction power FP is the difference, and mechanical efficiency is the ratio of the two.
IP, BP and FP are in the same unit, usually kW; η<sub>mech</sub> is a pure number, often given as a percentage.
Brake power is computed from two measured quantities, torque and speed.

blocks.where: BP is brake power in W; T is the torque absorbed by the dynamometer in N·m; N is engine speed in rev/min; the factor 2π/60 converts rev/min to rad/s. Divide by 1000 for kW.

blocks.text: Torque and speed are read directly, so BP is never in doubt. IP needs a pressure record or a Morse test; FP needs a motoring test, a Willans line or a subtraction. The dynamometer itself is in the chapter on dynamometers.

sections.h3: Indicated power from the p-V loop

items: Record cylinder pressure against volume for one full cycle of one cylinder.
The area inside the closed loop is the net work per cycle, to the pressure and volume scales.
Measure the area in mm² with a planimeter, or count squares.
Divide the area by the diagram length in mm to get the mean height in mm.
Multiply the mean height by the indicator spring constant in bar/mm or kPa/mm. That is the imep.

blocks.text: imep is indicated mean effective pressure in kPa; V<sub>d</sub> is swept volume of one cylinder in m³; N is speed in rev/min; n<sub>R</sub> is 2 for a four-stroke and 1 for a two-stroke; IP is in kW for one cylinder. Multiply by the number of cylinders.
n<sub>R</sub> is the number of revolutions per power stroke. A four-stroke fires once in two revolutions, so at the same speed and imep it gives half the power of a two-stroke.

The old mechanical indicator scratched the loop on a card; a modern engine uses a piezoelectric transducer and a crank-angle encoder to draw the same loop in software (see the chapter on testing standards and pressure measurement. On a four-stroke the record has two loops: the large power loop of compression and expansion, and the small pumping loop of the exhaust and intake strokes, traced the other way round. Net imep comes from the power-loop area minus the pumping-loop area.

sections.h3: Morse test: cut one cylinder at a time

blocks.text: The Morse test works on engines with three or more cylinders. Hold speed and load fixed and note BP with all cylinders firing. Cut the ignition (SI) or fuel (CI) of cylinder 1 only; the engine slows, so reduce the dynamometer load until the speed is back at the same value. Note the new BP. Repeat for every cylinder.

blocks.where: BP is brake power with all k cylinders firing in kW; BP<sub>i</sub> is brake power with cylinder i cut in kW; the drop BP − BP<sub>i</sub> is the indicated power of that one cylinder.

items: Assumption 1: friction power is the same whether a cylinder fires or not.
Assumption 2: the firing cylinders deliver the same power as before the cut.
Assumption 3: the speed is brought back to the same value for every reading.
Then FP = IP − BP and η<sub>mech</sub> = BP/IP. FP must come out small and positive.
Weakness: it needs a multi-cylinder engine, and in a petrol engine cutting one cylinder disturbs the mixture and exhaust flow of the others, so readings must be taken quickly.

blocks.text: The motoring test measures friction directly. Couple the engine to a dynamometer, switch off fuel and ignition, and drive it at the test speed. The dynamometer then reads the power needed to turn it over, which is the friction power. It is quick and works on a single-cylinder engine. Weakness: with no combustion the walls, piston and oil are cooler and no gas pressure pushes the rings out, so the friction measured is not the friction at running temperature.

Willans line uses fuel flow. Hold speed constant and vary the load. Plot fuel consumption rate in kg/h against BP in kW. At moderate and heavy load the points lie on a straight line. Extend it to zero fuel flow: it meets the BP axis at BP = −FP, so the size of that negative intercept is FP. The assumptions are a straight line and friction power independent of load. Near zero load the line curves because combustion becomes poor, so only the straight part may be extrapolated. See the chapter on fuel and air measurement for the fuel-flow measurement.

spec.aria: Plot of fuel flow against brake power with four points on a straight line, extended to zero fuel at minus 3.75 kilowatts.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine runs at constant speed. BP with all four cylinders firing is 20.0 kW. Cutting each cylinder in turn and restoring the same speed gives brake powers 14.2, 14.0, 14.3 and 14.1 kW. Find IP, FP and mechanical efficiency.
steps: Cylinder 1 cut: drop = BP − BP₁ = 20.0 − 14.2 = 5.8 kW, so cylinder 1 indicates 5.8 kW.
Friction power FP = IP − BP = 23.4 − 20.0 = 3.4 kW.
examples.answer: IP = 23.4 kW, FP = 3.4 kW and η<sub>mech</sub> = 85.5 %.
examples.check:
bp = 20.0
cut = [14.2, 14.0, 14.3, 14.1]
drops = [round(bp - c, 1) for c in cut]
ip = round(sum(drops), 1)
fp = round(ip - bp, 1)
eta = round(100 * bp / ip, 1)
print(ip)
print(fp)
print(eta)

examples.question: A diesel engine runs at a constant 1500 rpm. At brake powers of 5, 10, 15 and 20 kW its fuel flow is 2.10, 3.30, 4.50 and 5.70 kg/h. Find the friction power by Willans line, and the indicated power and mechanical efficiency at 20 kW.
steps: Slope of the line: (5.70 − 2.10) ÷ (20 − 5) = 3.60 ÷ 15 = 0.24 kg/h per kW. Each step of 5 kW adds 1.20 kg/h, so the four points lie on one straight line.
Equation: ṁ<sub>f</sub> = 2.10 + 0.24 × (BP − 5) = 0.90 + 0.24 BP, with ṁ<sub>f</sub> in kg/h and BP in kW.
Extend to zero fuel flow: 0 = 0.90 + 0.24 BP, so BP = −0.90 ÷ 0.24 = −3.75 kW.
Friction power is the size of that intercept: FP = 3.75 kW, taken as the same at every load at this speed.
examples.answer: FP = 3.75 kW; at 20 kW, IP = 23.75 kW and mechanical efficiency 84.2 %.

traps: Adding the four cut readings (56.6 kW) instead of the four drops. A cut reading still contains the brake power of the other cylinders.
Reporting a negative friction power. FP is small and positive; a negative value means a cut reading was copied wrongly or BP was noted with the wrong number of cylinders firing.
Using N instead of N/2 in the indicated power formula for a four-stroke. That doubles IP, so the efficiency you calculate is half the true value: the 85.5 % example would come out near 43 %.
Mixing units in IP = imep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>). Use kPa with m³, or convert bar to kPa (×100) and litres to m³ (×10⁻³).

quiz.q: Define indicated power, brake power and friction power in one line each.
quiz.a: IP is the rate of work by the gas on the piston; BP is the rate of work at the shaft; FP is IP − BP, the power spent on the engine's own friction and auxiliary drives.

quiz.q: A single-cylinder four-stroke engine has a swept volume of 0.0006 m³ and runs at 2400 rev/min. The imep from its indicator diagram is 700 kPa. Find the indicated power.
quiz.a: n<sub>R</sub> = 2, so power strokes per minute = 2400/2 = 1200. IP = imep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>) = 700 × 0.0006 × 2400/(60×2) = 700 × 0.0006 × 20 = 8.4 kW.

quiz.q: A six-cylinder engine develops 90.0 kW with all cylinders firing. Cutting cylinders in turn gives 71.0, 70.5, 71.5, 70.8, 71.2 and 71.0 kW. Find IP, FP and mechanical efficiency.
A Willans line at constant speed meets the brake power axis at −2.6 kW. What does this tell you, and why does the line curve near zero load?
quiz.a: The magnitude of the negative intercept is the friction power, so FP = 2.6 kW. At very light load the mixture is poor and a large share of the fuel goes on losses that do not scale with power, so the straight-line law fails.

quiz.q: The motoring test on a cold engine gives a higher friction power than the Morse test on the same warm engine. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Cold oil is more viscous, so bearing, piston and ring friction is larger, and cooler walls keep the oil film colder and thicker still. (The missing gas pressure behind the rings works the other way, so a warm motoring test reads slightly low.)

quiz.q: State the three assumptions of the Morse test.
quiz.a: Friction power is unchanged when a cylinder is cut; the firing cylinders deliver the same indicated power as before the cut; the speed is brought back to the same value for every reading.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engine plants run an automated motoring test at the end of the line, comparing the torque trace with a stored signature to catch a tight bearing or wrong cam timing. Search for motoring friction test and COV of imep.
